effect_estimate.comment: Descriptive spatial-population estimates and qualitative legal/policy analysis reported; no regression point estimates, confidence intervals, or p-values are estimated.
effect_estimate.value: Descriptive geospatial/demographic estimates and qualitative policy analysis (no inferential statistical effect estimate reported): In 2022 (N = 4,560,000 residents), only 31% of Nairobi's population had good household sanitation (23% [1,050,000] sewered household toilets [HT/SEWER]; 8% [350,000] regularly emptied household tanks [HT/RT]), 26% used intermediate shared systems (23% [1,050,000] shared sewered [ST/SEWER]; 3% [150,000] container-based [CONTAINER]), and 44% relied on inadequate sanitation (30% [1,370,000] unsafely managed household toilets [HT/NC]; 10% [450,000] unsafely managed shared toilets [ST/NC]; 2% [70,000] public toilets; 2% [70,000] coping/open defecation), while citywide sewerage coverage remained stagnant at 50% since 2015. Despite constitutional right-to-sanitation recognition and pro-poor rhetoric, national and county laws, plans, and budgets disconnect climate adaptation from sanitation and subsidise centralised sewerage while omitting institutional mandates and public finance for non-sewered sanitation. Under a 2030 business-as-usual projection (N = 6,130,000), good household sanitation declines proportionally to 28% (22% [1,340,000] HT/SEWER; 6% [370,000] HT/RT), shared sewered reaches 34% (2,100,000), container-based reaches 4% (230,000), and 34% (2,090,000 residents) remain in inadequate sanitation regimes vulnerable to climate-driven flooding and water shortages.

mechanism_certainty.comment: Appraised under the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework (design ceiling = 2). Assigned 2 because the study directly documents and analyses specific legal, regulatory, planning, and budgetary instruments in Nairobi/Kenya (e.g., Constitution, Water Act, Climate Change Act, CIDP, NIUPLAN, NWMP, WASREB guidelines, NCWSC/AWWDA plans, and Mukuru Special Planning Area planning-regulation suspension) and how their sewer-centric design and omission of non-sewered governance/subsidies shape sanitation service regimes.

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: The study is a legal/policy/planning and investment document analysis combined with secondary geospatial socio-technical regime mapping and demographic scenario projection, without primary human-subjects qualitative interviews/surveys or a quasi-experimental intervention comparator; it therefore fits the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework rather than CASP, MMAT, JBI, or ROBINS-I.

sample_size.comment: Single-city case study using 100m x 100m WorldPop gridded population rasters across 8 sanitation service regimes (4,560,000 population in 2022; 6,130,000 projected in 2030) and 3 East Africa climate scenarios; the exact numeric count of reviewed legal, policy, planning, and investment documents is listed in Supporting Information S1-S3 Tables and not stated as a total N in the main text.
